a: my son Methuselah
p: The Dream Visions are framed as Enoch teaching his son, the way the Astronomical Book ends.
b: Chapters 83–90 are called the Book of Dream Visions. Like the end of the Astronomical Book (see 79:1; 82:1) and the Epistle (see 91:1), they are framed as Enoch passing his knowledge to his son Methuselah (Ge'ez Matusala), who is to hand it on to later generations. Genesis gives Methuselah only a birth and a death (Genesis 5:21–27). Here he is the first link in a chain of teachers, which is how the scribes behind 1 Enoch saw their own role.

a: I saw the first when I was learning to write
p: Jewish tradition made Enoch the first human to learn writing. Jubilees says the same.
b: Genesis never says Enoch wrote anything. But by the 200s BC Jews remembered him as the first person to learn writing and wisdom, and so as the one who wrote down the secrets of heaven. Jubilees 4:17 says he was the first on earth to learn writing and knowledge, and Jubilees 4:19 adds that he saw in a vision of his sleep what had happened and what would happen, which sounds like a summary of these two dreams. 1 Enoch also calls him "the scribe" (see 12:4).

a: I saw two visions before I married
t: Two dreams, two books in one
p: The first dream (83–84) is about the Flood. The second (85–90) retells all of history with animals.
b: The section has two dreams. The first, short one (chapters 83–84) shows the earth collapsing into the abyss, and Enoch prays that a remnant will survive: it is the Flood. The second, long one (chapters 85–90) is the "Animal Apocalypse," which tells the whole history of the world from Adam to the end with animals standing for people. Both are set before Enoch's marriage, that is, before Methuselah was born (Genesis 5:21), so Enoch is shown seeing the whole future in advance.

a: my grandfather Mahalalel
p: In Genesis 5 the line runs Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch. So Mahalalel is Enoch's grandfather.
b: Genesis 5:12–18 gives the line Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch. The Ge'ez spells the name Mälalʾel. Nothing else is told about him in Genesis. Here he plays the wise elder who hears the boy's nightmare and tells him what it means and what to do: pray. In Genesis 5's numbers Mahalalel would still have been alive in Enoch's youth.

a: I saw the earth swallowed up in a great abyss
p: The Flood is pictured as the sky falling and the earth sinking: creation running in reverse.
b: Genesis describes the Flood as the waters above and below breaking in (Genesis 7:11). Enoch's dream goes further: the sky itself falls, the earth sinks, mountains pile up and trees are torn out. It is creation coming undone. Later Jewish and Christian writers used the Flood the same way, as a picture of the final judgment (Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 3:5–7). Enoch's own closing words tie the two dreams together (90:42).

a: a word fell into my mouth
p: A Semitic way of saying words came to him without planning. It is not yet a prophecy.
b: The Ge'ez idiom wädqä nägär wəstä ʾäfuyä means that words came out before he thought: he cried out in his sleep. The same verb, "fall," is used of the sky falling in 83:3–4, so the falling sky makes a word fall into his mouth. The Plain keeps the picture because it is vivid and clear.
orig: ወድቀ ፡ ነገር ፡ ውስተ ፡ አፉየ (wädqä nägär wəstä ʾäfuyä)

a: the hidden things of all the sin of the earth
p: The Ge'ez word means hidden things. The dream reveals what sin is secretly doing to the world.
b: Ḫəbuʾat means "hidden things" or "secrets." The idea is that the earth's sin is invisible to people but known in heaven, and the dream uncovers it. In 1 Enoch the Watchers taught humans "secrets" they should not have known (see 8:3; 16:3), so the word carries a charge: the hidden sin of the world is tied to hidden knowledge that came down from rebel angels.

a: plead with the Lord of glory, since you are a man of faith
p: Genesis has no one pray for the world before the Flood. Here Enoch's prayer is why a remnant survives.
b: In Genesis, Noah "found favor" (Genesis 6:8), but no one prays for the world. This passage adds that the boy Enoch was told to pray, did pray (84:1–6), and was heard: Noah's family is the "remnant" he asked for. That goes beyond Genesis without contradicting it, and it fits a pattern in the Bible of righteous people pleading for others, such as Abraham for Sodom (Genesis 18:22–33) and Moses for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14). Readers who receive the book as Scripture can take it as one more example of the prayers of the righteous (James 5:16). Other churches note that Genesis itself gives no such prayer.

a: the Lord of glory
p: One of 1 Enoch's titles for God. The New Testament uses the same phrase for Jesus.
b: 1 Enoch uses many titles for God; this part has "the Lord of glory" (83:8), "the Lord of judgment" (83:11), "the Holy Great One" (84:1), "the Lord of the sheep" (from 89:16) and "the Lord of righteousness" (90:40). Paul says the rulers of this age "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8), and James speaks of "Jesus Christ, our Lord of glory" (James 2:1). Whether they knew Enoch's phrase or both drew on Psalm 24:7–10 ("the King of glory") cannot be known.

a: everything as he had known it from the beginning
p: After the nightmare, the ordinary sunrise is proof that God still holds the world in order.
b: Enoch walks outside and sees sun, moon and stars keeping their courses. The steady order of the sky is a sign that God has not yet let the world fall. This links the Dream Visions to the Astronomical Book just before it, which is about the laws the lights obey (see 72:1). It also echoes God's promise after the Flood that day and night will not stop (Genesis 8:22). "He had known it" may mean God planned it so from the start.

a: windows of the east
p: 1 Enoch pictures gates or windows in the edge of the sky where the sun comes in and goes out.
b: The Astronomical Book describes six "gates" in the east and six in the west through which the sun rises and sets during the year (see 72:2–3). "Windows" here is that picture. Ancient readers took it as a model of the sky, much as Genesis speaks of the "windows of the sky" (Genesis 7:11). Most modern readers, whatever they think of the book, read such language as describing how the sky looks to a person standing on the earth.

a: the Holy Great One
p: A title of God found all through 1 Enoch.
b: The Ge'ez has qədus wäʿäbiy, "the Holy and Great." The site renders the title "the Holy Great One" everywhere in 1 Enoch (see 1:3). It joins Isaiah's favorite name for God, "the Holy One of Israel," with God's greatness, and it is the first of several titles in this prayer.

a: a tongue of flesh
p: Enoch stresses that he is only flesh. The same words open his prayer for the Watchers in 14:2.
b: Enoch says he speaks "with a tongue of flesh" that God gave to humans for speaking. The same phrase introduces his report to the Watchers (see 14:2). The point is that the gift of speech is God's, and a creature uses it rightly when it blesses its maker. Compare Psalm 51:15 and James 3:9–10.

a: King of kings
p: Babylon's kings used this title. Daniel gives it to Nebuchadnezzar; the New Testament gives it to Christ.
b: "King of kings" was a title of Mesopotamian and Persian rulers (Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:37). Jewish prayer claimed it for God, the true king over all kings. In the New Testament it is a title of Jesus (1 Timothy 6:15; Revelation 17:14; Revelation 19:16). Enoch's prayer is one of the earliest Jewish uses of it for God.

a: the whole earth is the footstool for your feet
t: Heaven a throne, earth a footstool
p: Isaiah 66:1 says the same, and Jesus quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: The picture comes from Isaiah 66:1, where God says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool. Jesus uses it to forbid swearing by heaven or earth (Matthew 5:34–35), and Stephen quotes it against the idea that a building can hold God (Acts 7:49). Enoch's prayer uses it to say that a God who fills all things can certainly save the earth.

a: No deed is too hard for you, not even one
p: The same faith as Jeremiah 32:17 and the angel's words to Mary in Luke 1:37.
b: Jeremiah prays that nothing is too hard for God (Jeremiah 32:17, 27), and God asks Abraham, "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14). Luke echoes the same words when the angel tells Mary that nothing is impossible with God (Luke 1:37). The Ge'ez adds wäʾi ʾäḥädu, "not one," after "deed": not even one. The feminine "one" (ʾäḥäti) that follows belongs with "wisdom," a feminine noun, in the next line.

a: Not one bit of wisdom leaves you
p: Jewish writers pictured Wisdom sitting beside God's throne.
b: Proverbs pictures Wisdom beside God at creation (Proverbs 8:27–31). The Wisdom of Solomon prays, "Give me Wisdom, who sits beside you on your thrones" (Wisdom of Solomon 9:4). 1 Enoch's Parables say Wisdom found no home on earth and went back to heaven (see 42:1–2). This prayer says the same Wisdom never leaves God's presence, so God knows exactly what to do with a sinful world.

a: the angels of your heavens are doing wrong
p: This is the Watchers' story of chapters 6–16, which the prayer treats as the cause of the Flood.
b: The verb yəʾebsu means "they sin, do wrong." The prayer assumes the story told in chapters 6–16: angels came down, took human wives and taught forbidden arts (see 6:1–8; 8:1–4). In 1 Enoch that rebellion is the main reason for the Flood. Genesis 6:1–4 tells the story of "the sons of God" in four verses and then gives human evil as the reason (Genesis 6:5).

a: set it up as a plant that grows from seed forever
p: A favorite picture in 1 Enoch for the faithful people God plants and keeps.
b: 1 Enoch often calls God's faithful people a plant: "the plant of righteousness and truth" (see 10:16), and in the Apocalypse of Weeks Abraham's family becomes "the plant of righteous judgment" (see 93:5). The image comes from the prophets: Israel as the planting of the LORD (Isaiah 60:21; Isaiah 61:3). Enoch asks God to save a seed from the Flood. The Animal Apocalypse that follows shows how that seed grows.

a: I saw another dream
p: The second dream retells history from Adam to the end with animals. Every human is an animal.
b: Chapters 85–90 are called the Animal Apocalypse. In it, people are animals: the righteous line from Adam to Isaac are white cattle, Israel are sheep, the nations are wild animals and birds of prey, and God is "the Lord of the sheep." Angels appear as humans ("white men"), and fallen angels as stars. Only Noah and Moses "become men" (89:1; 89:36). No one is named: the reader has to decode it from the Bible's own story. See the table in the chapter pages for each animal and whom it stands for.

a: Edna
p: Genesis does not name Enoch's wife. Jubilees and 1 Enoch both call her Edna.
b: The Ge'ez is ʾƎdna. Jubilees 4:20 also says Enoch married Edni (Edna), the daughter of Danel. Genesis names none of the wives in Seth's line. Jewish retellings of Genesis like Jubilees often filled in such names.

a: A bull came out of the earth, and that bull was white
p: Adam is a white bull "from the earth," as in Genesis 2:7 God formed him from the ground.
b: Almost all interpreters agree that the first white bull is Adam. He comes out of the earth, just as in Genesis 2:7 God forms Adam from the ground. White marks the righteous line and is the color of the end, when all become white again (90:38). Bulls, the strongest farm animals, stand for the chosen line from Adam to Isaac. From Jacob on, Israel are sheep (89:12).

a: a young cow came out
p: The Ge'ez says a female calf. Charles's "heifer" says the same.
b: The Ge'ez ṭaʿwa ʾänsətiyawit is "a female calf," that is, a young cow (Charles: "a heifer"). She is Eve, who "came out after" Adam, as in Genesis 2:21–22. The two calves with her are Cain and Abel, called ṭaʿwa, "calves," not full-grown bulls.

a: One of them was black, and one was red
p: Black marks sin and the line of Cain. Red marks the blood of Abel.
b: The black calf is Cain and the red calf is Abel. Black stands for sin in this vision (Cain's line are black, 85:8). Red stands for blood: Abel is the first to die by violence. Of Noah's sons, one is later "red like blood" (89:9). The colors tell the reader how to judge each animal before any act is described.

a: The black calf gored the red one
p: Genesis 4:8 in animal form. The vision says nothing about Cain's offering or God's question.
b: Genesis tells it this way: "Cain turned on Abel his brother and killed him" (Genesis 4:8). The vision keeps only the violence: goring and chasing. It skips the two offerings, God's warning and God's question to Cain (Genesis 4:3–15). That is typical of the Animal Apocalypse: it picks out the events that show who is violent and who suffers.

a: that young cow came with him
p: Probably Cain's wife, though the wording could also mean Eve.
b: "That young cow" seems to point back to the young cow of 85:3, Eve. But it makes better sense as Cain's wife, who "went with him" as he moved away. Genesis never says where Cain's wife came from (Genesis 4:17). Jubilees 4:9 says he married his sister Awan, and many read this verse the same way. Others think the vision is simply careless here.

a: she wailed over him bitterly
p: Genesis says nothing of Eve's grief. The vision adds it, and adds that Adam comforted her.
b: Genesis moves from Abel's death to Seth's birth with Eve's words that God gave her another child "instead of Abel" (Genesis 4:25). The vision adds a scene of Eve searching and wailing until Adam comforts her (85:7). It goes beyond Genesis, but it is the kind of feeling Genesis 4:25 implies. Later Jewish and Christian retellings of the story of Adam and Eve also describe her grief over Abel.

a: she gave birth to another white bull
p: The second white bull is Seth, born after Abel's death to replace him.
b: Genesis 4:25 and 5:3 tell of Seth's birth. He is white, like Adam: the righteous line goes through him. The "many cattle and black calves" born after him fit Genesis 5:4, which says Adam had other sons and daughters. The black ones are those who followed Cain's way.

a: They began to father many white cattle
p: This verse sums up Genesis 5, the line from Seth to Enoch.
b: "One after another" sums up the long list of Genesis 5: Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah. Enoch, the one dreaming, never appears as an animal in his own dream until he is lifted out of the earth (87:3). In Charles's English this verse is printed as part of 85:9.

a: a single star fell from the sky
p: The first fallen star is Asael (Azazel), the angel who taught forbidden arts in 8:1.
b: In the Bible stars can stand for angels (Job 38:7; Judges 5:20; Daniel 8:10; Revelation 1:20). The single star that falls first is usually identified with Asael, called Azazel in later copies, who in chapter 8 teaches weapon-making and cosmetics (see 8:1) and in 10:4 is bound first. Revelation has a similar picture: "I saw a star that had fallen out of the sky onto the earth" (Revelation 9:1). Many Christian readers have connected the falling star of Isaiah 14:12 with Satan, but 1 Enoch does not make that link.

a: It got up and ate and grazed among those cattle
t: Two stories of the fall, in order
p: First one star falls, then many. The vision orders two strands of the Watchers story.
b: Scholars see two strands in chapters 6–11: one about Shemihazah and his two hundred angels who took wives (see 6:1–8), another about Asael, who taught forbidden arts (see 8:1–3). The Animal Apocalypse puts them in order: first one star falls and lives among humans (Asael), then many stars come down to him (86:3). Some think this ordering is the writer's own way of joining the strands.

a: they began to moan, one with another
p: The Ge'ez says "moan." Charles took it as "began to live with each other."
b: The verb yäʿawyəwu normally means "to wail, moan" (as in 89:20). Charles translated it as the cattle "began to live with each other," reading the verse as the two lines of Seth and Cain mixing. The Plain keeps the usual sense: when the star arrives, the cattle's settled life is upset, and they groan. The scene is still debated.

a: many stars come down
p: The two hundred Watchers of 6:6, here as stars. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 know the same story.
b: These are the angels who came down on Mount Hermon (see 6:6). Jude 6 speaks of "the angels who did not keep to their own rank, but deserted the dwelling that was theirs" (Jude 6), and 2 Peter 2:4 of angels God sent to Tartarus. Genesis 6:2 says only that "the sons of God" took wives. Whether Jude and 2 Peter depend on 1 Enoch or on the same tradition is debated (see the book page).

a: bring out their private parts like horses
p: A crude picture taken from the prophets' language about unfaithfulness.
b: The image is blunt on purpose. Jeremiah calls unfaithful Judah "well-fed stallions" neighing after their neighbors' wives (Jeremiah 5:8), and Ezekiel uses a still cruder picture of horses' lust (Ezekiel 23:20). The vision uses it to show angels acting like animals in heat: holy beings have become beasts.

a: elephants, camels and donkeys
p: The giants are huge, mixed animals, unlike the cattle. Some Greek copies of 1 Enoch list three kinds of giants.
b: The children of stars and cows are not cattle but elephants, camels and donkeys: large animals that are not the same kind as their mothers. They are the giants of Genesis 6:4, "the Nephilim" (see 7:2). The number three may match the Greek of Syncellus at 7:2, which lists three kinds, giants, Nephilim and Elioud, and Jubilees 7:22. The Ge'ez words are nägeyat, ʾägmal and ʾäʿdug.

a: Then they began to eat those cattle
p: This retells 7:3–5, where the giants eat everything humans have, then humans themselves.
b: In chapter 7 the giants eat up the people's food and then turn on the people (see 7:3–5). Genesis says only that the earth was "filled with violence" (Genesis 6:11). The vision shows that violence as predators eating farm animals.

a: beings who looked like white men
p: In this vision humans are animals and angels look like men. Four are the archangels of chapter 9.
b: The code works by moving everyone one step down: people are animals, so angels look like people. Daniel too sees angels "like a man" (Daniel 8:15; Daniel 10:5) and calls Gabriel "the man" (Daniel 9:21). The four who come first (the Ge'ez numeral reads "one" here; see the variant) are the four archangels of 9:1, usually Michael, Sariel (or Uriel), Raphael and Gabriel. The three who come with them make seven, the seven holy angels of 20:1–8 (compare Tobit 12:15; Revelation 8:2).

a: lifted me away from the generations of the earth
p: Genesis 5:24 says God took Enoch. Here three angels lift him to a high place to watch history.
b: Genesis says only, "Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Hebrews reads that as being taken so that he did not see death (Hebrews 11:5). The vision makes it a lifting to a high place, from which Enoch watches the rest of history. Enoch has not appeared as an animal before this point; he enters his own dream only as the one taken out of it. Elijah will later join him there (89:52).

a: a tower high above the earth
p: Later in the vision a tower is the Temple. This one is probably God's dwelling in heaven.
b: In 89:50 and 89:73 "the tower" is the Temple in Jerusalem, where the Lord of the sheep stands. Here, before any temple exists, the high tower is probably God's own dwelling or paradise, where Enoch is kept. Some see a hint that the earthly Temple copies a heavenly one (compare Exodus 25:9; Hebrews 8:5).

a: tied its hands and feet, and threw it into an abyss
p: Raphael binds Asael in 10:4. The New Testament pictures rebel angels and Satan bound the same way.
b: In 10:4 Raphael is told to bind Asael hand and foot and throw him into the darkness. Jude 6 says God keeps rebel angels "in everlasting chains down in the gloom" (Jude 6), and 2 Peter 2:4 says much the same. Revelation pictures Satan bound in the abyss: "He threw him into the abyss and shut it and sealed it over him" (Revelation 20:3). The same picture of binding until the final judgment runs through all of them.

a: One of them drew his sword and gave it
t: The giants turned on each other
p: Gabriel's task in 10:9: set the giants against one another.
b: In 10:9 Gabriel is sent to stir up a war of destruction among the giants, so that they kill each other. Here the angel hands them a sword. In 1 Enoch the giants destroy themselves before the Flood comes. Jubilees 5:9 tells the same story.

a: threw stones from the sky
p: The Ge'ez verb means to stone or throw. Charles kept "stoned (them)."
b: Wägärä means "he threw stones." It may picture a storm of stones like the hailstones of Joshua 10:11, or simply mean the angel struck the stars down. The angel is Michael, who in 10:11–12 binds Shemihazah and his company under the earth for seventy generations.

a: taught him a secret, while he trembled
p: In Genesis God speaks to Noah himself. In 1 Enoch an archangel brings the warning.
b: In Genesis 6:13 God speaks directly to Noah. In 1 Enoch an archangel brings the message (see 10:1–3, where Sariel or Uriel is sent to Noah). This goes beyond Genesis but does not deny it: in 1 Enoch angels often carry out God's word. On "while he trembled" see the variant.

a: he became a man
p: Only Noah and Moses "become men." Most read it as being raised to an angel-like role.
b: In this vision men stand for angels, so a bull "becoming a man" means something special. Only Noah (here) and Moses (89:36) are changed this way, and both build something at God's command, the boat and the "house." Most interpreters say they are given an angel-like role or knowledge. Others think it simply means they were given a job for God. The Aramaic copy 4Q206 from Qumran has pieces of 88:3–89:6, according to Milik. Their readings have not been checked for this page.

a: He built himself a great boat
p: The Ge'ez word means a boat or vessel. Genesis' Hebrew word means a box.
b: Genesis calls Noah's craft a tevah, a box or chest (Genesis 6:14), the same word used for the basket of baby Moses (Exodus 2:3). The Ge'ez here uses mäsqär, "vessel, boat." The English "ark" comes from the Latin arca, "chest." The Plain says "boat" because the Ge'ez does.

a: I saw a high roof with seven torrents on it
p: The roof is the sky. Seven channels pour water into an enclosure, the earth.
b: Genesis says that "all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11). The vision shows both: torrents from a high roof (89:2) and springs from below (89:3). The world is an enclosure, a cattle pen, and the cattle inside are drowned. Seven means the waters are complete.

a: the cattle, elephants, camels and donkeys sank
p: Genesis says all flesh died. 1 Enoch says the giants died too.
b: Genesis says every living thing outside the ark died (Genesis 7:21–23). 1 Enoch says the giants, the elephants, camels and donkeys, drowned with them. This agrees with Wisdom of Solomon 14:6, which says the proud giants perished. It goes beyond Genesis, which never says the giants were in the Flood. And it conflicts with Numbers 13:33 if the spies' report of Nephilim in Canaan after the Flood is taken literally; many readers take that report as the frightened scouts' exaggeration. Within 1 Enoch it also sits uneasily with 88:2 and 10:9, where the giants kill each other first.

a: One of the three was white like that bull
p: The white son is Shem. The red and black ones are Ham and Japheth, though which is which is debated.
b: "Noah's sons who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham and Japheth" (Genesis 9:18). Shem is white: the chosen line runs through him to Abraham. The red and black ones are Ham and Japheth. Many think red is Ham and black Japheth; others reverse them. Only Shem matters for what follows, and "that white bull left them" means Noah's death (Genesis 9:29).

a: nations of many kinds
p: The Ge'ez lets slip what the animals are: "kinds of nations."
b: The Ge'ez says the animals were "ḫəbrä ʾäḥzab," "kinds of nations." For a moment the code is broken: the wild animals and birds are the peoples of the world. Genesis 10 lists seventy nations descended from Noah's sons. In the vision they are unclean animals, predators and scavengers, while Israel will be sheep, a clean animal. Most scholars see Leviticus 11's clean and unclean animals behind the choice.

a: rock badgers
p: The Ge'ez word probably means the rock hyrax. Charles guessed "squirrels."
b: Gəḥe is usually taken as the hyrax, a small rock-dwelling animal (the "coney" or "rock badger" of Leviticus 11:5 and Psalm 104:18). Charles rendered it "squirrels." Several of these animals reappear later as particular nations: dogs, foxes and wild boars in 89:42, lions, leopards, wolves and hyenas in 89:55, eagles, vultures, kites and ravens in 90:2.

a: a white bull was born
p: Abraham, born among the nations. The vision skips Babel and God's call.
b: The white bull born among the beasts is Abraham, who came from a family of the nations (Joshua 24:2). The vision skips the Tower of Babel, God's call (Genesis 12:1–3) and the covenant (Genesis 15; Genesis 17). It is interested in lines of descent, white and not white, more than in covenants.

a: a wild donkey and a white bull
p: Ishmael is a wild donkey because Genesis 16:12 calls him one.
b: The angel tells Hagar that Ishmael will be "a wild donkey of a man" (Genesis 16:12), and the vision takes the words literally. The white bull is Isaac. The wild donkeys who "grew many" are the Ishmaelite tribes (Genesis 25:12–18). Later the Midianites are counted with them (89:13; 89:16), as in Genesis 37:28.

a: a black wild boar and a white sheep
t: Esau the boar, Jacob the sheep
p: Esau, father of Edom, is a black boar. Jacob is the first sheep: from him on, Israel are sheep.
b: Esau is a boar, an unclean animal (Leviticus 11:7), perhaps because Psalm 80:13 speaks of a boar from the forest ravaging God's vine. His descendants, the Edomites, are "many boars." Jacob is the first sheep, and his twelve sons are twelve sheep. Later Jewish writers called Rome "Edom" and sometimes pictured it as a pig. The change from cattle to sheep may show that Israel is a smaller people under a shepherd (Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1).

a: twelve sheep
p: The twelve tribes' fathers. Israel is a flock from here to the end of the vision.
b: Jacob's twelve sons (Genesis 35:22–26) are twelve sheep. From now on God's people are a flock, and the whole rest of the vision is a story of sheep, their "Lord," their shepherds and the beasts that attack them.

a: they handed one of them over to the donkeys
p: Joseph sold to the Ishmaelites and taken to Egypt. The wolves are the Egyptians.
b: Joseph's brothers "sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and they took Joseph to Egypt" (Genesis 37:28). The donkeys are Ishmaelites and Midianites; the wolves are the Egyptians. "Grew up among the wolves" covers Joseph's whole rise in Egypt (Genesis 39–41) without a word about it.

a: threw their young into a river of deep water
p: Exodus 1:22, told from the sheep's side.
b: Pharaoh ordered, "Every son who is born, you must throw into the Nile" (Exodus 1:22). The vision tells it from the victims' side: the sheep cry out and complain to their Lord, as Israel cried out in Exodus 2:23–25.

a: went over to the wild donkeys
p: Moses flees to Midian, whose people the vision counts as wild donkeys like the Ishmaelites.
b: "Moses ran from Pharaoh and went to live in the land of Midian" (Exodus 2:15). The Midianites were children of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), so the vision files them with the wild donkeys, Abraham's other non-Israelite descendants.

a: the Lord of the sheep came down
p: God's name in the rest of the vision. It comes from the Bible's picture of God as Israel's shepherd.
b: From here God is ʾƎgziʾä ʾäbagʿ, "the Lord of the sheep," that is, their owner. The Bible often calls God Israel's shepherd (Genesis 48:15; Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1; Ezekiel 34:11–16), but the vision saves "shepherd" for the seventy angels who misrule (89:59). "Came down" echoes God's words at the burning bush: I have come down to rescue them (Exodus 3:8).

a: Another sheep met that sheep
p: Aaron meets Moses, and the two go to Pharaoh's court.
b: Exodus 4:27 says, "Aaron went, met him at God's mountain and kissed him." The "meeting of those wolves" is Pharaoh's court (Exodus 5:1). The vision folds the ten plagues into a single line: "Their Lord came to the sheep and began to strike those wolves" (89:20).

a: The wolves' eyes were blinded
p: The key image of the whole vision: open eyes mean knowing God, blind eyes mean turning from him.
b: Here Pharaoh's people are blinded, as in Exodus God hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 14:4). From now on blindness and sight run through the story: Israel opens its eyes in the wilderness (89:28), goes blind at the golden calf (89:32), sees and goes blind under the judges (89:41), goes blind before the exile (89:54) and after it (89:74), and only the lambs open their eyes (90:6). At the end, everyone sees (90:35).

a: the water stood up on this side and on that side
p: The crossing of the sea, with the Lord standing between his flock and the wolves.
b: Exodus says the waters split apart (Exodus 14:21), and the Song of the Sea says "Running streams stood up like a mound" (Exodus 15:8). The Lord standing between the sheep and the wolves is the pillar of cloud moving behind Israel (Exodus 14:19–20). The sea "became as it had been created" (89:26) when it closed again.

a: giving them water and grass
p: Manna and water from the rock, in sheep's terms.
b: In a desert with no water or grass, the Lord gives water and grass: the manna (Exodus 16), the quail and the water from the rock (Exodus 17:1–7). "They began to open their eyes and to see": in the wilderness, Israel first comes to know its God.

a: the top of that high rock
p: The vision tells of Sinai but never mentions the Law given there. Scholars debate why.
b: The high rock is Mount Sinai. The vision tells of Moses going up, God appearing, the people afraid, and the golden calf. But it never says that God gave the Law. Some scholars think the writers' group put Enoch's revelation ahead of Moses' Law, or at least did not center their faith on it. Others answer that an animal story cannot easily show a law code, and that "the path he had shown them" (89:32) means the Law. Readers who keep both Moses' books and Enoch as Scripture, as the Ethiopian Orthodox churches do, naturally read it the second way.

a: We cannot stand in front of our Lord or look at him!
p: Israel's terror at Sinai, as in Exodus 20:19 and Deuteronomy 5.
b: At Sinai the people begged Moses to speak to them instead of God (Exodus 20:18–19; Deuteronomy 5:23–27). God himself told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Hebrews 12:18–21 uses the same scene to contrast Sinai's terror with the welcome of the new covenant.

a: to wander from the path he had shown them
p: Israel goes blind and wanders off while Moses is on the mountain.
b: This is the golden calf (Exodus 32:1–8): while Moses is on the mountain, the people turn away. The calf itself is not shown, perhaps because an animal story about a statue of a calf would be confusing. "Wander" (səḥtu) becomes the vision's word for turning away from God (89:33; 89:35; 89:51).

a: He began to kill them
p: Exodus 32:26–28: Moses and the Levites kill those who worshiped the calf.
b: Moses called, "Whoever is on the LORD's side, to me!" and "About three thousand of the people fell that day" (Exodus 32:26–28). The "other sheep" Moses takes with him are the Levites. The vision does not soften the story. It treats the killing as bringing the strays back to the fold.

a: He built a house for the Lord of the sheep
p: The "house" first means the tabernacle and Israel's camp. Later it is Jerusalem.
b: Moses builds a "house" for the Lord and puts all the sheep in it: the tabernacle and the camp around it (Exodus 25–40). In the land, the house becomes Jerusalem, and a "tower," the Temple, is built on it (89:50). Scholars debate whether "house" always means the city, or sometimes the Temple. The Aramaic copy 4Q204 preserves pieces of 89:31–37, according to Milik.

a: the sheep who had met the sheep that led them fell asleep
p: A gentle word for death. Aaron dies first, then the whole wilderness generation.
b: "Fell asleep" means died, as often in the Bible (Daniel 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13). Aaron, who met Moses (89:18), dies first: "Aaron died there on the top of the mountain" (Numbers 20:28). Then the large sheep die and small ones replace them, the generation that left Egypt dying in the desert (Numbers 14:29–31). The river is the Jordan.

a: went away from them and fell asleep
p: Moses "went away" before he died. Some see a hint of a hidden grave or an assumption.
b: "There in the land of Moab, Moses the servant of the LORD died" (Deuteronomy 34:5), and "The Israelites wept for Moses on the plains of Moab for thirty days" (Deuteronomy 34:8). "Went away from them" fits Deuteronomy 34:6, where no one knows his grave. Some see the later Jewish belief that Moses was taken up, which was told in a lost ending of the Testament of Moses. But the vision says he "fell asleep": he died.

a: And there rose up sheep to lead them
p: The Ge'ez says "all" the leaders rose up. Charles's English has "the two sheep."
b: On "all" or "two" see the variant. Either way, Joshua leads the people across the Jordan (Joshua 3–4) into the land.

a: a pleasant and glorious land
p: Canaan, the "beautiful land" of Daniel and Jeremiah. The house is now the tabernacle at Shiloh.
b: Jeremiah calls Israel's land "a pleasant land" (Jeremiah 3:19), and Daniel calls it "the beautiful land" (Daniel 8:9; Daniel 11:16; Daniel 11:41). The final throne will be set up in this same "pleasant land" (90:20). The house among them is the tabernacle in the land (Joshua 18:1).

a: Sometimes their eyes were open, and sometimes they were blind
p: The book of Judges in one sentence: faithful, unfaithful, rescued, again and again.
b: Judges tells a repeated cycle: Israel turns away, is oppressed, cries out, and God raises a judge (Judges 2:11–19). "Another sheep" who brings them all back is usually taken as Samuel, the last judge (1 Samuel 7:3–17), though some see the judges in general.

a: dogs, foxes and wild boars
p: The dogs are the Philistines. The foxes and boars are usually taken as Ammon and Edom (or Amalek).
b: Most interpreters take the dogs as the Philistines, Israel's chief enemy under Saul and David (1 Samuel 13–31). The foxes are often taken as the Ammonites and the wild boars as the Edomites (Esau was a boar, 89:12), or as the Amalekites. Saul fought all of them (1 Samuel 14:47–48).

a: a ram, who led them
p: A ram leads the flock. Saul is the first ram.
b: The Ge'ez ḥärge is a ram, the male that leads a flock. Kings are rams: Saul (89:42–47), David (89:45–48) and Solomon (89:48). Daniel also pictures a king as a ram (Daniel 8:3–4, 20). Notice that in this vision kings are never "shepherds": that word is kept for the seventy angels.

a: Then dogs, foxes and wild boars began to eat
p: A Greek summary of 89:42–49 survives in shorthand in a Vatican manuscript. It is older than the Ethiopic.
b: Apart from Ethiopic, 89:42–49 also survives in Greek: a passage written in Byzantine Greek shorthand in a Vatican manuscript, printed by Angelo Mai and deciphered by Johann Gildemeister in 1855. It is not a plain copy but a quotation inside another work ("next to these it is written that...", 89:47), and it shortens as it goes. It agrees with the Ethiopic in outline, but it has "the Lord of the sheep raised up" the ram (89:42), "left its way" where the Ethiopic has "gave up his glory" (89:44), calls Samuel and David "lambs" (89:45), and has nothing about Solomon in 89:48. See the variants on those verses. Parts of 89:43–44 are also in the Aramaic copy 4Q205, according to Milik.

a: The ram gave up his glory
p: Saul fails and turns on his own people. Samuel sees it.
b: The sheep "whose eyes were opened" is Samuel. Saul "gave up his glory" by disobeying (1 Samuel 13:13–14; 1 Samuel 15:22–28), and he "trampled" his own sheep: he killed the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:17–19) and hunted David. "Today the LORD has ripped Israel's kingship off you and given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you" (1 Samuel 15:28).

a: raised that one up to be a ram
p: Samuel goes to David privately and anoints him king.
b: "Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him there among his brothers" (1 Samuel 16:13). "Spoke to him alone" (89:46) fits that quiet anointing. Charles's English calls both sheep "lambs" here, following the Vatican Greek (arna); the Ge'ez has the ordinary word for sheep.

a: until those dogs brought the first ram down
p: Saul chases David, then falls in battle with the Philistines.
b: Saul hunted David (1 Samuel 18–26), and David fled. Saul died fighting the Philistines on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:1–6). The vision does not mention that Saul fell on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:4): the dogs brought him down.

a: a little sheep became ram in his place
t: Solomon, and the order of verses
p: Solomon follows David. Charles moved this sentence after 89:49; the Ethiopic has it here.
b: The "little sheep" who becomes ram is Solomon (1 Kings 1:28–40). In the Ethiopic manuscripts the sentence about David's death and Solomon comes here, before the summary of victories in 89:49. Charles thought it out of place and printed it after 89:49 as "89:48b." The Vatican Greek runs straight from the second ram's leading (89:48) to the flock's growth (89:49) without it (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Ethiopic order. Then 89:49 sums up the peace that David's wars won for the kingdom (2 Samuel 8:1–14; 1 Kings 4:24–25).

a: A high tower was built on that house for the Lord of the sheep
p: The house is Jerusalem, and the tower is Solomon's Temple, where God "stands."
b: Jerusalem grows "large and wide," and a tower is built for the Lord: Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6–8). Isaiah's song of the vineyard also has a tower built in the vineyard (Isaiah 5:2), and Jesus' parable repeats it (Mark 12:1). "The house was low, but the tower was high": the Temple stood on the hill above the city. The full table is the offerings (compare Malachi 1:7, "the LORD's table").

a: the sheep began to kill them
p: The sent sheep are prophets. Israel's killing of its prophets is a theme Jesus takes up.
b: Elijah complained, "They have killed your prophets with the sword" (1 Kings 19:10). Nehemiah's prayer confesses the same (Nehemiah 9:26). Jesus speaks of Jerusalem as the city "that kills the prophets" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 11:47–51). The vision shows the whole period of the kings this way.

a: He brought it up to me and had it stay here
p: Elijah is rescued and brought up to where Enoch is. He returns at the end (90:31).
b: Elijah escaped Jezebel (1 Kings 19:1–3) and was later taken: "Elijah went up to the heavens in the windstorm" (2 Kings 2:11). The vision says he was brought up "to me," to Enoch's high place. Enoch and Elijah, the two people the Bible says did not die, are kept together and come back before the judgment (90:31). On their return together and the two witnesses of Revelation 11, see 90:31.

a: betrayed his place
p: The Ge'ez may mean they handed over God's place, Jerusalem, to its enemies.
b: The verb ʾägbəʾu can mean "caused to return" or "handed over." Charles translated "betrayed His place." The idea is that by leaving God's house they gave up Jerusalem to destruction. The "slaughter in their flocks" covers the Assyrian and Babylonian wars against both kingdoms.

a: lions, leopards, wolves and hyenas
p: The Ge'ez word is the leopard. Charles's "tigers" is a looser rendering.
b: The Ge'ez ʾänamrət is the leopard (Hebrew nemer, as in Jeremiah 5:6 and Hosea 13:7); Charles's "tigers" is a looser rendering. The lions and leopards are usually taken as the Assyrians and Babylonians, the wolves as Egypt (as in 89:13), the hyenas and foxes as smaller neighbors such as Ammon and Moab. Which animal is which nation is debated.

a: he left that house of theirs and their tower
p: Ezekiel sees God's glory leave the Temple. Jesus says the house is left desolate.
b: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD leave the Temple before Babylon destroys it (Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 11:22–23). Jesus warns Jerusalem that its house is left to it (Matthew 23:38). The Epistle of Barnabas quotes words very close to 89:56 and 89:66 as "Scripture": in the last days the Lord will hand over the sheep of the pasture, their fold and their tower to destruction (Barnabas 16:5). On this point Enoch agrees with the prophets.
r: Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 11:22–23; Matthew 23:38; Epistle of Barnabas 16:5

a: I began to cry out with all my strength
p: Enoch, watching from heaven, pleads for the sheep, as he once pleaded for the earth (83:10).
b: The dreamer cannot stay neutral. As a boy he prayed for the earth (84:1–6); now he cries for the sheep. Later he weeps over what he has seen (90:41). Readers in the 160s BC, suffering under foreign rule, could hear their own prayers in his.

a: He was glad that they were eaten
t: Did God rejoice in Israel's ruin?
p: Deuteronomy 28:63 speaks this way. Ezekiel says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
b: This is a hard line. It agrees with Deuteronomy 28:63, which warns that the LORD will take delight in destroying a disobedient Israel. But it conflicts with Ezekiel 33:11, where God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and with Lamentations 3:33, which says he does not willingly afflict. Readers who defend the line take it, as they take Deuteronomy 28:63, as a picture of God's justice against sin, not of cruelty. Other readers note that the vision quickly blames the shepherds for going beyond God's orders (89:61; compare Zechariah 1:15).

a: He called seventy shepherds
p: Most scholars: angels set over Israel during foreign rule. Some older scholars: Gentile kings.
b: Most scholars since Charles take the shepherds as angels. They are given Israel to rule from the exile to the end, are called to account by God, and are thrown into the fire with the fallen stars (90:25). Behind them stand the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 and the flock meant for slaughter in Zechariah 11:4–17, and the old belief that God set heavenly beings over the nations: "to match the number of the sons of God" (Deuteronomy 32:8). Some older scholars took them as Gentile kings, and a few as Israel's own leaders. Seventy recalls Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11), which Daniel 9:24 stretched to seventy weeks of years.

a: the shepherds and their companions
p: The Ge'ez word means partners or assistants. Each shepherd seems to have helpers.
b: Ḍämad means "yoke-partner, companion." The shepherds' "companions" appear again in 89:68. They may be lower angels who serve under each shepherd, or a second group of rulers. The text does not explain.

a: He called another one
t: The angel who keeps the record
p: An angel writes down what each shepherd does. He is one of the seven white ones (90:22).
b: The recorder is "one of the seven white ones" (90:22) and later comes down to help Judas Maccabeus (90:14). Many identify him with Michael, the prince who stands for Israel (Daniel 10:21; Daniel 12:1). Others think of Raphael or simply an unnamed archangel. In the Bible, God keeps books of deeds (Malachi 3:16; Daniel 7:10).

a: Write down every excess
p: Every deed is written down, to be opened at the judgment (90:20).
b: God keeps books: Daniel sees that "the books were opened" (Daniel 7:10), and Revelation says "books were opened" (Revelation 20:12). Here the books record the shepherds' deeds, counted against each one, and they are opened at the throne in 90:20.

a: so that I may hand them over
p: "Them" may be the sheep, handed to the shepherds, or the shepherds, handed over for judgment.
b: The Ge'ez kämä ʾəmäṭwomu (Dillmann; the EOTC has wäʾmäṭwomu) means "that I may hand them over." It is not clear who "them" are. It may be the sheep, whom God hands to the shepherds, or the shepherds themselves, whom God will hand over for judgment once the record shows what they did (90:22–25). The Plain keeps the open "them."

a: Do not let them know
p: The prophets say the same: God used nations to punish Israel, but held them guilty for cruelty.
b: The shepherds are told to destroy some sheep but destroy far more, and they are not warned that a record is kept. The prophets say the same of the nations: Assyria was God's rod but meant more harm than God sent (Isaiah 10:5–7); Babylon showed no mercy (Isaiah 47:6); and God says, "I was only a little angry, but they helped make the harm worse" (Zechariah 1:15). Enoch agrees with them, but goes beyond them by placing angels, not just nations, under that judgment.

a: They burned that tower and tore down that house
p: Babylon burns the Temple and tears down Jerusalem.
b: "He set the LORD's house on fire, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem" (2 Kings 25:9). Babylon's army broke down the walls (2 Kings 25:10). The "wild boars" eating with the lions may be Edom, which joined in Jerusalem's fall (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7).

a: Each of them received a counted number in his time
p: The seventy shepherds rule in four groups: 12, 23, 23 and 12.
b: The vision counts the shepherds in four groups: 12 by 89:72; 23 more, for 35 in all by 90:1 (the Ethiopic says 37, see the variant there); 23 more, for 58 by 90:5; and 12 more by 90:17, making 70. Most scholars match them to the Babylonian, Persian, early Greek (Ptolemaic) and Seleucid eras, from about 587 to the 160s BC. The numbers are schematic rather than exact years.

a: the one who was writing
p: Babylon and Egypt pictured gods who wrote down fates. Here an angel records the shepherds' deeds.
b: Ancient peoples imagined scribe-gods who kept the records of heaven, such as Nabu in Babylon and Thoth in Egypt. Jewish writers gave that job to an angel. Enoch himself is called a scribe (see 12:4), and Jubilees 4:23 says Enoch writes down the world's judgment.

a: for twelve hours
p: Each shepherd's period is called an "hour" here. The twelve are the periods of the first twelve shepherds, the exile.
b: The Ge'ez says the shepherds pastured "twelve hours" (säʿat). It means the periods of the first twelve shepherds, the Babylonian exile from 587 to about 539 BC. Then three sheep return: usually Zerubbabel, Jeshua the high priest, and Nehemiah or Ezra, though some count Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:8–11; Ezra 3:2).

a: The wild boars tried to stop them
p: The boars may be Edomites or the Samaritans who opposed the returning exiles.
b: Ezra says, "the people of the land worked to break the courage of the people of Judah" (Ezra 4:4). Since boars stood for Edom (89:12), some think of Edomites, who had moved into southern Judah. Others see the Samaritans, Nehemiah's opponents (Nehemiah 4:1–8).

a: all the bread on it was defiled and not pure
p: The vision says the rebuilt Temple's worship was impure from the start. That conflicts with Haggai, Zechariah and Ezra.
b: This is one of the sharpest lines in 1 Enoch. Malachi attacked priests who offered defiled bread (Malachi 1:7), but he did not reject the Temple itself. Haggai, Zechariah and Ezra present the rebuilt Temple as God's will, built at his command and dedicated with joy (Haggai 1:8; Haggai 2:9; Ezra 6:14–16). Here the worship is defiled from its first day. On this point 1 Enoch conflicts with those books. Many scholars connect it with the calendar of the Astronomical Book (see 72:32) and with groups who thought the Temple's priests kept the wrong times; the Dead Sea Scrolls show similar complaints. Readers who hold both as Scripture can read the line as a judgment on the priests' practice in the writer's own day rather than on the Temple God commanded.

a: mixed in with the animals
p: Jews living among the nations, and blending into them.
b: After the exile, many Jews stayed in Babylon, Egypt and elsewhere. Ezra complains that some had married into the peoples of the land (Ezra 9:1–2). "Mixed in with the animals" may picture both the scattering and the loss of a separate life.

a: He pleaded with him for them
p: Zechariah 1:12 has an angel ask God how long he will withhold mercy, after seventy years.
b: The recording angel not only accuses the shepherds but pleads for Israel. Zechariah saw the angel of the LORD ask, "How long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem," seventy years after its fall (Zechariah 1:12). In Daniel, Michael stands for Israel (Daniel 12:1). Angels who pray for the righteous appear often in 1 Enoch (see 9:1–11).

a: eagles, vultures, kites and ravens
t: The Greek age: birds of prey
p: When Alexander's Greeks arrive, the beasts give way to birds. The ravens are usually the Seleucids.
b: The change from wild animals to birds of prey marks the coming of the Greeks after Alexander the Great (332 BC). Most scholars take the eagles as the Macedonian Greeks in general, the ravens as the Seleucid kings of Syria (whose king Antiochus IV persecuted the Jews), and the vultures and kites as the Ptolemies of Egypt or other Greek powers. Daniel likewise gives the Greek beast wings (Daniel 7:6).

a: until only their bones were standing
p: A picture of cruelty borrowed from Micah, and a hint of Ezekiel's dry bones.
b: Micah accuses Israel's rulers of tearing the skin off the people and the flesh from their bones (Micah 3:2–3). Ezekiel saw a valley of bones brought back to life (Ezekiel 37:1–14). The vision's people are reduced to bones, ready for God's new start.

a: fifty-eight periods in all
p: The running total of shepherds' periods. It is why most scholars correct 90:1 from 37 to 35.
b: "Fifty-eight" is a running total: the shepherds of 89:72 and 90:1 plus these 23. It only works if 90:1 has 35 shepherds, not 37. For the full count see 89:68 and the variant at 90:1.

a: little lambs were born to those white sheep
p: A new group around 200 BC who "open their eyes." Many think it is the writers' own movement.
b: The lambs who see while others stay blind are a reform movement in Judea in the early 100s BC. Many scholars identify them with the "Hasideans," the pious who joined the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:42; 1 Maccabees 7:13), or with the group behind 1 Enoch itself, the "chosen righteous" of the Apocalypse of Weeks (see 93:10). The Damascus Document from Qumran tells a similar story: a group like blind men groping their way, until God raised a teacher.

a: They seized one of those lambs
p: Many think of the high priest Onias III, murdered around 170 BC.
b: Charles and many since think this is Onias III, the lawful high priest, who was removed and then murdered around 171–170 BC by an agent of the Seleucid court (2 Maccabees 4:30–38). Daniel 9:26 speaks of "an anointed one" cut off, often read the same way. Others say the vision means a death we cannot identify.

a: one great horn sprouted
p: Most scholars identify the great horn with Judas Maccabeus, who led the revolt from 166 BC.
b: A horn stands for power and leadership (Psalm 132:17; Daniel 7:8; Daniel 8:5). Almost all scholars since Charles identify the great horn with Judas Maccabeus, who led the Jewish revolt against Antiochus IV from 166 BC until his death in 160 BC (1 Maccabees 3:1–9). Some nineteenth-century scholars, writing before the Aramaic copies were found, took it as John Hyrcanus (ruled 134–104 BC). The oldest Aramaic copy of the Dream Visions, 4Q207, is dated by Milik to about 150–125 BC, which makes so late a date unlikely.

a: the rams saw it
p: A second Ge'ez word for a male animal. The "rams" are the leaders who rally to Judas.
b: The Ge'ez here is dabela, a different word from the ḥärge used for Israel's kings in 89:42. It means a male of the flock, a ram or he-goat. The lambs with horns have grown into rams: leaders who rally to Judas, as his brothers and the faithful rallied to Mattathias's family (1 Maccabees 2:42–48; 1 Maccabees 3:1–2).

a: they could not overpower it
p: Judas defeats the Seleucid generals Apollonius and Seron.
b: 1 Maccabees 3:10–26 tells of Judas's early victories against the Seleucid commanders Apollonius and Seron, and then against Gorgias at Emmaus (1 Maccabees 4:1–25). The ravens, the Seleucids, fight the horn but cannot break it.

a: until the shepherds came
p: The great push against Judas: probably Lysias's campaign of 164 BC.
b: The shepherds, eagles, vultures and kites all join the ravens: a major campaign against Judas. Many take it as the army of the Seleucid regent Lysias, defeated near Beth-zur in 164 BC, shortly before Judas cleansed the Temple (1 Maccabees 4:26–35; 2 Maccabees 11:1–12).

a: His help had come down to that ram
p: 2 Maccabees says a rider in white appeared and led Judas's army near Beth-zur.
b: 2 Maccabees 11:6–10 says that as Judas's army set out near Beth-zur, a horseman dressed in white, with gold weapons, appeared at their head, and they charged. The vision says the recording angel came down to help the ram. The two stories seem to remember the same belief: that heaven fought for Judas. The angel is probably Michael, Israel's prince (Daniel 12:1).

a: fell into his shadow
p: An odd phrase. It may mean the enemies fell into darkness before God's face.
b: The Ge'ez ṣəlalot means "shadow." To "fall into his shadow" is strange; Charles kept it. It may mean the enemies fell into darkness, or that they were overshadowed and crushed. The Dillmann text says "his shadow"; the EOTC text says "the shadow."

a: They all came together and helped each other
t: A doublet, and the date of the vision
p: 90:13–15 and 90:16–18 tell almost the same battle twice. This helps scholars date the vision.
b: Verses 13–15 and 16–18 both have the enemies gather against the horn and God come in anger. Charles thought one was added later. Many now think the writer updated his own work as the war went on. Either way, the real history seems to stop around here: the vision knows Judas's battles in 164 BC but not his death in battle in 160 BC (1 Maccabees 9:5–22). So most scholars date the Animal Apocalypse to about 164–160 BC, with older parts perhaps written a little before. From 90:17 on, the vision moves from history to hope.

a: the last twelve shepherds
p: The twelve last shepherds are the Seleucid period, the age of the writer's own day.
b: The last twelve shepherds bring the total to seventy (see 89:68). They are the Seleucid kings' era, roughly 200 BC to the writer's day. They destroy more than all before them: the persecution of Antiochus IV, who banned the Law and set up a pagan altar in the Temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:41–64).

a: the rod of his anger
p: God strikes the earth, and it opens and swallows the nations' armies.
b: The "rod of my anger" in Isaiah 10:5 is Assyria, used against Israel; here God takes the rod into his own hand against the nations. The earth opening and closing over them recalls Korah's rebels (Numbers 16:31–33). Psalm 2:9 speaks of the Lord's king breaking the nations with an iron rod.

a: a great sword was given to the sheep
p: The vision backs the armed revolt. Daniel, from the same years, seems more cautious.
b: The sheep receive a great sword and drive out all the beasts: the vision supports Judas's armed revolt and expects it to end in God's victory. Daniel, written in the same years, calls the Maccabees only "a little help" (Daniel 11:34) and expects the wise to suffer and wait (Daniel 11:33–35; Daniel 12:1–3). Daniel and 1 Enoch differ on fighting, but this is not a conflict with the 66 books as a whole, which contain both holy war (Joshua 6; 1 Samuel 15) and patient waiting. Enoch goes beyond Daniel in giving the faithful a sword. It is sealed up once the war is over (90:34).

a: a throne was set up in the pleasant land
p: Like Daniel 7:9–10, but on earth, in the land of Israel.
b: Daniel sees thrones set up, the Ancient of Days seated, and books opened (Daniel 7:9–10). Revelation sees a great white throne, and "books were opened" (Revelation 20:12). Jesus speaks of the Son of Man on his glorious throne judging the nations (Matthew 25:31–33). In Enoch's vision the throne stands in the "pleasant land," Israel itself, and the books are the shepherds' records (89:62–71).

a: The other one took all the sealed books
p: The Ge'ez verb has no named subject. "The other one," the recording angel, is supplied, as Charles does.
b: The Ge'ez says only wänäśʾä, "and he took." Since the books are opened "before the Lord of the sheep," the one who takes them is probably not the Lord himself but the angel who kept the record (89:61; 90:14; 90:22). The Plain supplies "the other one," as Charles does.

a: those seven first white ones
p: The seven archangels of 20:1–8 bring the fallen stars to judgment.
b: These are the seven "white men" of 87:2, the archangels named in 20:1–8. Tobit 12:15 speaks of seven angels who stand before God, and Revelation 8:2 of "the seven angels who stand in front of God." The first judged are the stars, starting with the first one that fell (86:1).

a: full of blazing fire and full of pillars of fire
p: The place of the fallen angels' punishment, which Enoch saw in 18:11 and 21:7.
b: Enoch saw this place on his journeys: a deep chasm with pillars of fire (see 18:11; 21:7–10). Jesus speaks of a fire that lasts forever, made ready for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Revelation speaks of a lake of fire for the devil, the beast and the false prophet (Revelation 20:10).

a: Those seventy shepherds were judged
p: The rulers of the nations' angels are judged too. Psalm 82 and Isaiah 24 say something similar.
b: Psalm 82 pictures God judging the "gods" who ruled unjustly and telling them they will die like humans (Psalm 82:1–7). Isaiah 24:21 says God will punish "the army on high, up on high." Paul says believers will judge angels (1 Corinthians 6:3). Enoch goes beyond these by naming seventy and counting their crimes, but the idea that heavenly powers answer to God is in the Bible itself.

a: That abyss was to the right of that house
p: "Right" means south. The fiery valley south of Jerusalem became Gehenna, the word for hell.
b: In Semitic directions you face east, so "to the right" means south. The valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, was cursed because children had been burned there to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31–32). In 1 Enoch it is the "cursed valley" (see 27:1–2), and in later Jewish and Christian speech Gehenna became the name for hell (Mark 9:43–48; compare Isaiah 66:24). Here the blinded sheep, the Jews who abandoned God, are judged there.

a: those blinded sheep
p: Faithless Jews share the fire with the fallen angels. The prophets warned of judgment on Israel too.
b: The "blinded sheep" are Jews who turned away, perhaps above all those who embraced Greek ways in the 170s–160s BC (1 Maccabees 1:11–15). Isaiah ends with the bodies of rebels against God lying outside Jerusalem (Isaiah 66:24), and Daniel 12:2 says some will rise to everlasting shame. Enoch agrees that judgment starts with God's own people (compare 1 Peter 4:17), and goes beyond the Hebrew Bible in the detail of a burning abyss.

a: they folded up that old house
t: The old house folded like a tent
p: Jerusalem is folded up and carried away like a tent. The tower, the Temple, is not even mentioned.
b: The old house, Jerusalem, is folded up like a tent and put away to the south. Isaiah pictures Jerusalem as a tent whose pegs will never be pulled up (Isaiah 33:20; Isaiah 54:2). Notice that the vision says nothing more about the tower: after 89:73 the Second Temple is never named again.

a: a new house, larger and higher than the first one
t: A new Jerusalem, with no temple?
p: God brings a new house. No tower, no temple, is mentioned. Revelation 21:22 also has no temple.
b: God himself brings the new house: "I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:2). Strikingly, the new house has no tower. The Temple-tower, rebuilt in 89:73 with defiled bread, is not replaced. Revelation agrees of the new Jerusalem: "I did not see a temple in it, because the Lord God, the Almighty, is its temple, and so is the Lamb" (Revelation 21:22). Ezekiel 40–48 and Tobit 14:5, by contrast, expect a rebuilt Temple. Some scholars think the whole new city is the Temple, since God dwells in it.

a: bowing to those sheep
p: The nations bow to Israel, as Isaiah promised. But then they are changed too (90:33, 90:38).
b: Isaiah promised that the nations would bow to Israel (Isaiah 49:23; Isaiah 60:14) and that peoples would come to Zion to learn God's ways (Isaiah 2:2–4; compare Zechariah 8:20–23). In the vision they first bow, then join the sheep in the house (90:33), and finally all become white cattle together (90:38).

a: with the hand of that ram holding me too
p: "That ram" is probably Elijah, taken up in 89:52. Enoch and Elijah come back together.
b: Enoch is set down among the sheep "before the judgment," though the judgment was just described: the vision is not in strict order here. "That ram" is puzzling, because the last ram was Judas. Most interpreters think it means Elijah, the sheep brought up to Enoch in 89:52, so the two men who did not die return together. Malachi 4:5 promises Elijah before the great day. Early Christian writers such as Tertullian and Hippolytus, and Ethiopian tradition, looked for Enoch and Elijah as the two witnesses of Revelation 11.

a: their wool was thick and clean
p: All God's people are white now: pure, like the first white bull.
b: White wool is the color of cleansing: "like snow they will turn white... like wool they will be" (Isaiah 1:18). The Ancient of Days has hair like pure wool (Daniel 7:9), and Revelation's saints wash their robes white (Revelation 7:14). In the vision, white marked the righteous from Adam on; now every sheep is white.

a: they had all become good and had come back to his house
p: The wild animals and birds gather in God's house too. Some read this as the conversion of the nations.
b: "All the wild animals and all the birds" gather in the house, and the Lord rejoices because all are good. Many scholars read this as the conversion of the Gentiles (Isaiah 56:6–8; Zechariah 14:16). Daniel Olson argues that the vision's climax is the fulfillment of God's promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Others think only the nations that did not oppress Israel are meant, since the oppressors were swallowed by the earth (90:18).

a: it was sealed up
p: When the war is won, the sword is sealed up in God's house. War is over for good.
b: The sword given to the sheep (90:19) is brought back and sealed before the Lord. Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 promise that nations will beat their swords into plows. The sheep do not keep their weapons; the peace of the new house needs none.

a: There was not one among them who could not see
p: The vision's long story of blindness ends: everyone sees.
b: Isaiah promised that the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5), and Jeremiah that all would know the LORD, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34). This verse closes the blindness theme that began with the wolves (89:21).

a: a white bull was born, with large horns
p: A new Adam at the end of history. Most call him a messiah, though he does almost nothing.
b: At the start a white bull was Adam (85:3). At the end a white bull is born again, with large horns, and all creatures fear him and pray to him. Most scholars call him a messianic figure, but a quiet one: he fights no battle and judges no one; he comes after God has done everything. Some see a new Adam, beginning a restored humanity. Many Christian readers, including readers in the Ethiopian Orthodox churches who receive the book as Scripture, have read him as Christ, the second Adam (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45). Daniel Assefa's study of the vision asks how far its ending serves the Maccabean war and how far it looks beyond it.

a: they all became white cattle
p: Sheep and beasts alike turn into white cattle, like Adam's line before Abraham's family.
b: In the vision only the line from Adam to Isaac were white cattle. Now Israel and the nations together become white cattle. The end returns to the beginning: one humanity, righteous, as before the split into nations and before Israel became a flock. The Epistle of Barnabas 6:13 has God say he makes the last things like the first. Compare the new creation of Isaiah 65:17 and Revelation 21:1–5.

a: The first among them
p: The Ge'ez says the first one became "a word." Charles read "lamb"; others "wild ox." Ethiopian readers hear John 1:1.
b: The Ge'ez nägär means "word." A word becoming an animal makes little sense in the code, so scholars look for a slip in translation. Charles printed "lamb," explaining "word" as Hebrew millah ("word") misread for taleh ("lamb"). Another proposal takes it as the Hebrew re'em, "wild ox," written in Greek letters and then mistaken for Greek rhēma, "word"; several modern commentators prefer this. Ethiopian Orthodox readers keep "word" and read it of Christ, the Word who became flesh (John 1:1, 14). See the variant on these words.

a: the Lord of righteousness
p: Enoch's last title for God in this book: the one whose justice the whole vision has shown.
b: ʾƎgziʾä ṣədq, "the Lord of righteousness," sums up the vision: God has judged the stars, the shepherds and the blind sheep, and rescued the faithful. Compare "the LORD our righteousness" (Jeremiah 23:6).

a: For everything will come and be fulfilled
t: Prophecy, or history written as prophecy?
p: Enoch weeps because he has seen all history in advance. Scholars and believers read this differently.
b: The vision claims to show all of history before it happens. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read it as true prophecy given to Enoch before the Flood. Most historians read it as history told in the form of prophecy, the way Daniel 11 is often read: exact up to the writer's own time (about 164–160 BC), then a hope for what God would do next. Both readings see its message: history is in God's hands, and he will finish what he began (Daniel 2:28).

a: That night I remembered my first dream
p: The Flood dream and the end-time dream belong together. The New Testament pairs them too.
b: At the end Enoch remembers the first dream, of the Flood (83:3–5). The two dreams belong together: the Flood was the first judgment, and the end will be the last. Jesus compares his coming to the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37–39), and 2 Peter 3:5–7 sets the world once destroyed by water beside the world kept for fire.
